chapter_theme: General songs (பொதுப்பாடல்கள், 21 of 21): short songs that ask for the knowledge that cuts 'I' and 'mine', for the experience (அநுபூதி) and dance of knowledge, for the vision of the feet beyond the river of births, the net of family and the women who want gold, and for knowledge no book can hold; three akam songs give the lovesick girl under Kama, the moon and the town's gossip, and the book ends on a fragmentary song of Murugan's hill and battle.
structure_note: Thirteen eight-line songs (1292 to 1304), of which 1296, 1297 and 1303 are akam; 1303 repeats the frame of 1290 in the previous chapter. 1305 is a long song printed with gaps (marked ...), apparently incomplete.

1292.reading: The poet asks not to think of serving women whose words are sweet as honey, and that he be given to know the understanding in which 'I' and 'mine' are cut away. The praise calls Murugan dear to Indra, king of the gods, younger brother of the elephant-faced one, the six-faced lord.
1292.nuance: யான் எனது அற்றிடு போதம்: the same pair of 'I' and 'mine' that the Kural names as the root of bondage; here its cutting is asked as a gift of knowledge, not achieved by effort.

1293.reading: The poet asks not to think of desire for women but to seek Murugan's two lotus feet, and to be given the experience that is nectar, sugar and honey. The praise names him the cause of all, of excellent nature, who unites with the forest Kuratti, whose vel fought Sura's kin to dust, rider of the peacock.
1293.nuance: The sweetness the poet turns from (women) returns as the sweetness of அநுபூதி, nectar, sugar and honey (ஆரமுதமான சர்க்கரை தேனே). காரணமதான: Murugan as the cause.

1294.reading: The poet asks that to him, a poor one who seeks the dance of knowledge with a melting that grows every day, the wealth of experience may flourish. The praise calls Murugan the child given by Siva who wears poolai and erukku flowers, the moon and the snake, and the lord who called the elephant at the right moment.
1294.nuance: நாளும் மிகுத்த கசிவு: devotion as a melting that grows daily. ஞான நிருத்தம், the dance of knowledge, is the object sought. வேளை தனக்கு உசிதமாக வேழம் அழைத்த likely alludes to Murugan calling the elephant (Ganesa) to frighten Valli into his arms, but the text gives only the elephant and the timing.

1295.reading: The poet, thinking of and seeking Murugan daily, asks that with those who have attained nishtha as his companions, and by the path of their high austerity, he be given the dance of the aim and its marks. The praise calls him nephew of the conch-bearer Vishnu who sent destruction on the kin of the victorious rakshasas, dweller in the hearts of the faultless, bearer of the cock banner.
1295.nuance: நிட்டை பெற்று இயல் கருத்தர் துணையாக: the company of those established in contemplation is the means. லக்ய லக்கண நிருத்தம் may mean the dance that is both the goal and its sign; நத்தியு தமதவத்தின் is hard to split.

1296.reading: An akam plea, in the voice of the girl's mother or friend: having seen Murugan come in glory on his peacock like a dark blue cloud, the girl is infatuated, so let him give her the fragrant garland on his chest. The praise names the Vel who once hurled the vel at the sea, death to the clan of valiant Suras, meaning of the four Vedas, the lord who strikes his chest saying 'It is I'.
1296.nuance: மால்கொண்ட பேதை: the girl's infatuation began with a sight of the god's procession, and what is asked is his garland (தார்), the classical token of the hero's acceptance. நான் என்று மார் தட்டும் gives Murugan a warrior's boast.

1297.reading: An akam plea: is it right that the girl sink in sorrow because of Kama, who died yet did not die, the reproach of the women nearby, and moonlight that burns without burning? The praise calls Murugan the hero of unchecked strength, death to the arguing Sura clan, rider of the unrestrained peacock, the peerless lord.
1297.nuance: The plea is built on paradoxes: பட்டுப் படாத மதன், Kama burned by Siva yet alive, and சுட்டுச் சுடாத நிலவு, moonlight that scorches without fire. பக்கத்து மாதர் வசை is the town's gossip of akam poetry.

1298.reading: The poet asks Murugan to come and grant boons in plenty, so that he may become a master fit for Murugan's line, as his father was found fit to carry a message to Paravai again and again. The praise names him younger brother of the karpaka-like elephant god, husband of the Kuratti whose eyes are bows, the one who told Siva what was fitting, and who knocked Brahma on the head.
1298.nuance: பரவைக்கு எத்தனை விசை தூது: Paravai is the wife of the saint Sundarar, to whom Siva went as messenger at his devotee's bidding, and the plea asks for grace on that scale. அரனுக்கு உற்றது புகல்வோனே, அயனைக் குட்டிய: the teaching of Siva and the punishing of Brahma, the story elsewhere told of Om, which is not named here. The construction of the plea's first two lines is uncertain.

1299.reading: The poet asks not to enter the river of births with its waves nor wander on the path of nature, but by the meaning of the guru's sure word to be given the vision of Murugan's feet. The praise calls him the meaning of the scriptures of the six creeds, an ocean of virtue to those who know the knowledge within knowledge, the lord of the three Tamils whom the short sage Agastya praises, Kumaraguru of the Krittikas.
1299.nuance: பிரகிருதி மார்க்கம்: the path of nature, of the body and its tattvas, set against the guru's word (குரு வாக்கியப் பொருள்). அறுசமய சாத்திரப் பொருளோனே: here Murugan is the meaning the six creeds share, where 1287 and 1288 call sectarian devotion vain. குறுமுனிவன் ஏத்தும் முத்தமிழோனே: Murugan as Tamil, praised by Agastya.

1300.reading: The poet asks Murugan to think of revealing in grace the wise attainment of knowledge that cannot be completed by writing on the leaves of books, and of gently gathering him in and guarding him. The praise names him the one who won fame by honouring and praising the girl who dwells in the forest where parrots play, and who guarded the karpaka grove.
1300.nuance: புத்தகத்து ஏட்டில் தீட்டி முடியாது: the knowledge sought is beyond what can be written in a book, so it must be given by grace (அருளாலே). The line கைத்தலத் தீக்குப் பார்த்து நுழையாத is obscure; it may say the grove was one that (the demons) feared to enter.

1301.reading: The poet, who wavers desiring the meanness of public women who desire gold, asks that Murugan, desiring him, grant him once to desire to think of Murugan. The praise calls him the guru desired truly by Siva of the lightning-bright matted hair, who drew near and desired the Kuratti whom the mother desired.
1301.nuance: Every line turns on விரும்பு, desire: the women desire gold, the poet desires their meanness, Murugan is asked to desire the poet so that the poet may desire him, and Siva and Murugan desire in turn. The wordplay moves desire from gold to grace. பொதுமாதர் and பொன்னை விரும்பிய name the courtesans' trade.

1302.reading: Not knowing how to cross the net of maya called house, children and kin, swollen with his deeds, the poet, a dog of a servant, asks whether he must pour water on weeds. The praise calls Murugan bridegroom of the Kuratti who plays stirring up the spring, and the lord who cut the gods free from prison.
1302.nuance: மனை மக்கள் சுற்றம் எனும் மாயா வலை: the household itself is the net. விழலுக்கு இறைத்தல், watering useless grass, is a proverb for wasted effort, here the poet's whole life.

1303.reading: The girl speaks for herself: must this sinner's life faint because of the moon rising over the sea, the arrows Kama shot, and the reproach that has spread over the whole earth? The praise names the Vel that pierced Sura's broad chest, the light, the king seated on the peacock, the chest that wedded the elephant-maiden, the lord of the three gods and all the gods.
1303.nuance: பாவியேன் ஆவி மயங்கலாமோ is the girl's own voice, where 1290 speaks of her. பாரெலாம் ஏசிய: the gossip has spread over the whole world. மூரி மால் யானை may be Devayanai.

1304.reading: The poet asks not to be born into the deceptive false hut that sky, earth, wind, water and fire inhabit, but to learn Murugan's name with the Tamil of knowledge and attainment and to be given praise in his hand. The praise calls him the one bound to the forest Kuratti of rustic speech, the Vel that fought the golden mountain, wearer of the fragrant vetchi garland, emperor of the gods' heaven.
1304.nuance: மாயத் தெற்றிப் பொய்க்குடில்: the body as a false hut of the five elements. புகழ் கைக்குப் புரிவாயே may be read as asking for the gift of praise-songs, புகழ், the name of the book itself. The split of the first line (வானப் புக்குப் பற்றும் மருத்து) is uncertain.

1305.reading: The surviving lines invoke Murugan as guru, Saravanabhava, Shanmukha and Guha, delight of the hunter's daughter, lord of the kurinji hills where tigers, bears, boars, buffaloes and deer roam, and ask for his grace; then they describe drums, conches, horns and trumpets thundering as at the world's end while the world cries 'Hara Hara, Siva Siva, refuge', and end on the anklet-bearing feet that come to help devotees.
1305.nuance: The text is incomplete, so no plea survives beyond அருள் தருவாயே; the rest is a battle scene in instrument names and the closing image of the feet that come to the devotees (அன்பர்க்கு வந்து உதவு).

links.note: Both name 'I' and 'mine' (யான் எனது) as what must be cut; the Kural promises a world above the gods to whoever cuts them, and 1292 asks the cutting itself as a gift of knowledge.

In both the town's gossip feeds the girl's love-sickness rather than ending it; the Kural makes it manure for the sickness, and 1297 sets the reproach of women beside Kama and the moon as what sinks her in sorrow.
The same frame, the moon, Kama and a question ending -லாமோ, closing on தம்பிரானே; 1290 asks about the girl, 1303 is her own voice and adds the world's reproach.

source_issues: 1305: the song is printed with gaps marked ... and a broken line structure; parts of the text are missing.
1299 and 1305: a stray space after the vowel உ splits words at line starts (உ றுதி, உ னது, உ ழுவைகள், உ லவு, உ லகர்கள்).
